title: Karnataka Drought Deepens as CM Shivakumar Pleads With Modi for Central Aid
excerpt: With a 68% rainfall deficit, failing reservoirs and stalled kharif sowing, Karnataka's chief minister has written to the prime minister twice seeking urgent drought relief and a central assessment team.
body:
• Karnataka has recorded a 68% overall rainfall deficit, with 18 of 31 districts and 141 of 240 taluks facing deficient to severely deficient monsoon rainfall.
  • CM Shivakumar has written to PM Modi twice requesting a central team to assess the drought and provide financial assistance, with no response so far.
  • Kharif sowing stands at just 34% of the seasonal target, and the CM has asked farmers not to plant crops to conserve water for drinking.
  • Groundwater levels have dropped four metres in 88 taluks, and migration has begun from five northern Karnataka districts.

Karnataka is staring at one of its worst droughts in recent memory, with Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar escalating his appeals to Prime Minister Narendra Modi for urgent central intervention as the state's monsoon deficit reaches alarming levels.

The state has received only 203 mm of rainfall against a normal of 292 mm as of mid-July — a 30% deficit that has since worsened to 68%, according to Deputy Chief Minister G. Parameshwara. The India Meteorological Department has attributed the shortfall to strengthening El Niño conditions that have pushed sea surface temperatures up by roughly two degrees Celsius, while temperatures across Karnataka have risen by four to six degrees.

A State in Crisis

The numbers paint a grim picture. Of Karnataka's 31 districts, 18 are experiencing deficit to large-deficit rainfall. At the taluk level, 141 of 240 taluks have recorded deficient to severely deficient rainfall, and 75 taluks have endured dry weather for four consecutive weeks.

Kharif sowing has covered only 28.36 lakh hectares — a mere 34% of the seasonal target of 84.10 lakh hectares. Reservoir storage has fallen to 34% of capacity, and groundwater levels have dropped by approximately four metres across 88 taluks.

"The government is providing all necessary funds and support. Even after that, if any district witnesses hardship because of dereliction of duty, you will be held responsible."

— D.K. Shivakumar, Chief Minister, Karnataka

The crisis has pushed Shivakumar to take the extraordinary step of publicly advising farmers not to sow crops this season. He warned that insufficient rainfall and shrinking water reserves could lead to devastating crop losses and urged that available reservoir water be reserved strictly for drinking purposes.

Modi Yet to Respond

Shivakumar first wrote to PM Modi on July 15, requesting the immediate deployment of a central study team to assess the situation on the ground. The Union government has not yet responded, and the chief minister has announced he will write again to press for action.

An emergency Cabinet meeting was convened to review drought conditions, followed by a video conference with all Deputy Commissioners and Zilla Panchayat Chief Executive Officers. Shivakumar announced Rs 1 crore in immediate assistance for each taluk and directed Rs 329 crore already in the accounts of Deputy Commissioners to be deployed for relief.

The state government has also begun addressing rural migration from northern Karnataka districts including Ballari, Kalaburagi, Raichur, Yadgir and Vijayanagara, where residents have started leaving in search of employment.

Broader Stakes

Karnataka is India's second-highest tax-paying state, contributing approximately Rs 4.5 lakh crore annually to the national exchequer. Shivakumar has repeatedly argued that the Centre's financial allocations to the state fall well short of its contributions, making the drought crisis a test case for cooperative federalism.

Parameshwara described the situation as "unprecedented," noting that the number of villages dependent on tanker water supply was rising daily. Nearly 2,443 of approximately 5,000 Gram Panchayats have yet to commence works under the state's rural employment guarantee scheme.

For the Indian diaspora with roots in Karnataka, the drought raises concerns about the welfare of family members in rural areas and the economic ripple effects on the state's agriculture-dependent population. The crisis also carries national implications — Shivakumar has warned of disruptions to India's tur dal production, a staple pulse crop heavily concentrated in Karnataka's drought-affected northern districts.
nri_angle: Karnataka's severe drought raises concerns for diaspora members with family ties to rural Karnataka and could impact national food prices, particularly tur dal.
